newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major battles on despite defection blow.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major battles on despite defection blow.

text.p: Embattled British Prime Minister John Major fought to get off the political ropes on Monday after being jolted at the weekend by the fourth defection of a member of parliament in two years.
With a general election expected in May, Major's Conservatives were staggered by right-wing MP Sir George Gardiner's decision to join the Referendum Party of millionaire Sir James Goldsmith.
Gardiner's move followed his sacking by local Conservatives in the southern commuter town of Reigate as their election candidate.

It gives Goldsmith, who wants a referendum on Britain's future in the European Union, his first MP. Two Conservative parliamentarians had already defected to the minority Liberal Democrats and one to the main opposition Labour party.
The moves have helped to push Major into a three-seat minority in parliament and have played their part in putting the Conservatives some 20 points behind Labour in the opinion polls.
Appearing on an independent radio phone-in programme, Major dismissed the group Gardiner has joined as "a one-issue party with a remarkably shortsighted view".
Then he turned his fire on Labour for offering lightweight policies. "This is not a country where you can deal with long-term problems with short-term snappy solutions," he said.

Major, who has faced severe problems in uniting his party over Europe, insisted that calls from right-wingers such as Gardiner for him to rule out British membership of a single European currency were not in the country's interests.
He repeated his view that the time had not yet come to decide on the issue.
However, he said he would be prepared to use Britain's EU vote to stop countries joining a single currency if their economies were not ready for it.
"If they were likely to go ahead in the wrong circumstances, it is in the British national interest to stop them doing so," Major said.
If a single currency were "botched" without Britain joining it, the pound sterling could rise sharply against it. "That would make all our exporters uncompetitive," Major said.
Earlier, Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell announced details of radical proposals to transform care of elderly people which will be a key plank of the party election manifesto.

Dorrell announced that, if the Conservatives won a fifth consecutive term of office in May, they would introduce a new scheme to aid people needing long-term care in their old age, including cash from the state to supplement private health care insurance.
